findings.title: Omissions and form, not arithmetic
findings.deck: A diagnostic evaluation of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-sol, both at high reasoning effort, on {{tasks}} GDPval tasks, {{runs_each_word}} run each, with source-based grading and author review.
bullets: None of the {{confirmed_items}} confirmed failures is a wrong calculation.

The failures (failed rubric items) are content left out ({{omit_items}}), a different label or form ({{form_items}}), and one rounding approach that breaks an accounting rule ({{rule_items}}). Totals reconcile even where a breakdown is missing.
Only GPT-6.1-sol missed things the prompt asked for.

Each failure is tagged by whether the model was told: in the prompt; rubric only (GDPval's grading key expects it, the prompt doesn't say it); or the additions rule (ours, set before the runs). {{gpt_prompt_items}} of GPT-6.1-sol's {{gpt_items}} failures are in the prompt, such as store subtotals, and cost it {{gpt_prompt_task_fails}} tasks. All {{opus_items}} of Opus 5.5's are rubric only or the additions rule.
Rubric grading needs a human pass.

Of the {{rv_fail}} graded fails the author reviewed, chosen where a verdict could change ({{rv_fail_crit}}) or a model failure was suspected ({{rv_fail_draft}}), {{seg1}} ({{gff_pct}}%) were grader false fails; in {{fp_alone_word}} task a grader false pass hid the only failure. {{rubric_fail_cells}} of the {{fail_cells}} task failures ({{opus_tasks_fail}} Opus 5.5, {{gpt_tasks_fail}} GPT-6.1-sol) turn only on rubric-only wording or detail, or the additions rule.

M1: Required reporting levels or measures are omitted
The workbook has the inputs or higher-level totals but omits a requested measure or aggregation level.
ADDS: Neither prepaid schedule presents a per-line monthly additions column; the roll-forwards are arithmetically valid, and the rubric items fail under the additions rule (additions listed line by line).
R03: No separate indicator for a missing or invalid case pack (a rubric item beyond the prompt); no count is affected.
M2: Semantic substitutes miss an exact name or display the rubric specifies
The information is present, but the exact identifier, label, sheet name or decimal presentation the rubric names is replaced by another form.
M6: A grouped report lacks the prioritization the rubric asks for
The SKU summary cannot be sorted by total errors without breaking its grouping.
M3: An operational control or concrete validation step is left unspecified
The design or test document discusses the goal but leaves the named control, access decision or validation procedure unspecified.
M5: A nearby test scenario omits the exact required condition or assertion
A test covers the feature but not the required missing-input condition, specified fields or both-organisation edit.
M7: A plain-language explanation omits the rule it applies
The rule is applied correctly in the workbook, but the narrative leaves out the condition that defines it.
M4: A disclosed rounding adjustment conflicts with an accounting rule

A labelled fractional-cent line reconciles rounded lines to the exact balance and thereby shows negative amortization and a balance increase that no source document supports; the four rubric items are one rounding approach.

notes: Every item was confirmed by the author's review. Category C failures were all flagged first by the LLM judge or the blind audit, none by a code grader.
GPT-6.1-sol's two missing per-stop rubric items follow the expert reference's country-level approach; the rubric is stricter than the reference.

GPT-6.1-sol's six missing daily figures are the input to the weekly rate, which it reports correctly; that critical requirement passes. The failure type's high severity applies to the store subtotals and per-stop amounts.
A failure type seen once shows that the failure happened, not how often.

items.title: Example from A (Required content omitted): missing store subtotals
lines: The prompt asks the Sales by Store pivot table to "total the sales by store"; the rubric requires a labelled subtotal for each of the {{stores}} stores.
GPT-6.1-sol has the right grand total but no store subtotals; Opus 5.5 has all {{opus_store_total_rows}}.
Although the grand total is correct, the manager must reconstruct each store's total before comparing store performance.

items.title: Example from B (Label or display not as required): product names instead of UPC codes
lines: By the rubric, chart categories that are exactly the {{card_b_upcs_word}} UPC codes; the prompt asks which "products" have the highest out-of-stock rates.
Both models label the chart with product names; the UPCs appear only in tables.
Low: the chart answers the prompt's question but can't be matched to the UPC list. Exact labels like this decide {{m2_opus_sole}} of Opus 5.5's {{opus_failed_crit}} failed critical requirements.

items.title: Example from C (Document content omitted): the case-pack rule left out of a summary
lines: The prompt sets the rule (a CASE line must be ordered in whole multiples of the case pack) and asks for a Word summary "outlining the types of errors identified"; the rubric requires that summary to define both checks in plain language (rubric item {{c_item}}, critical).

Opus 5.5: a case-pack error is "a CASE-UOM line whose ordered units are not a whole multiple of the case pack". GPT-6.1-sol: "Case-pack errors count invalid CASE lines once; EA lines are exempt." It never says what makes a line invalid; "multiple" appears nowhere in its summary. Its workbook applies the rule correctly.
A manager can't tell from the summary why a line was flagged. The LLM judge passed this rubric item; only the blind audit caught it, and it alone fails GPT-6.1-sol's PO audit.

opus: a CASE-UOM line whose ordered units are not a whole multiple of the case pack
gpt: Case-pack errors count invalid CASE lines once; EA lines are exempt.

data.heading: Data opportunity
data.thesis: Models leave out pieces a task asks for, and the rubrics that grade them mix what a task needs with exact wording. The proposal: tasks where everything a deliverable must contain is listed, tagged with its source and verified by an expert, each with a deliberately broken version of the deliverable.
data.why_title: Why it has to be expert-verified (evidence from this evaluation)
why_points: {{seg1}} of the {{rv_fail}} graded fails the author reviewed were grader errors.
{{rubric_fail_cells}} of the {{fail_cells}} task failures turn only on rubric-only wording or detail, or the additions rule.
GDPval's own expert file for the weekly sales task fails two source checks: sell-through averaged over rows, and a Data tab that differs from the export in {{gold_cells}} cells.
data.card_lead: One sample = one professional task, with:
components: the task prompt and its real source files;

a checklist of everything the deliverable must contain (levels, measures, labels, controls, test conditions), each item tagged with its source (in the prompt, rubric only, or an evaluator's rule) and severity;
automated tests that compute expected values from the source files, and judge checks for explanations, controls and test conditions;
a deficient variant: the expert deliverable with one checklist item removed.
seed: The {{tasks}} tasks here, across {{occupations}} occupations, extended into task families: the same kind of work with fresh source data.

Built by domain experts. A second expert reviews each checklist. Every check passes on the expert deliverable. Each deficient variant fails the checks for the item it removes and passes the rest. Where a check and the expert disagree, a reviewer decides before the sample is accepted.
per_model: GPT-6.1-sol: what the prompt asks for first ({{gpt_prompt_items}} failures in {{gpt_prompt_tasks}} tasks, such as store subtotals). Opus 5.5: none of its failures is something the prompt asked for; of its {{opus_items}}, {{opus_detail_items}} are professional detail the rubric adds (environment separation, bucket versioning, a blank-date test case, sorting by error count, a case-pack flag), {{opus_wording_items}} exact wording and {{opus_rule_items}} the additions rule. Standards an expert knows but the prompt doesn't state are its opening; the suite also guards the breakdowns it delivers.
pilot: Grow {{pilot_families_n}} task families ({{pilot_families}}); in each, {{pilot_train}} tasks for training and {{pilot_heldout}} held out, on different source data; evaluate the held-out tasks, {{pilot_runs}} runs per task. Accept if the share of checklist items met rises by at least {{pilot_rise}} percentage points while the numerical tests' pass rate stays within {{pilot_hold}} points. Untested here.
cost: {{pilot_tasks}} tasks per family, {{pilot_samples}} samples. [GDPval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04374) reports {{gdpval_hours}} hours of expert work per task on average; with about {{pilot_extra_hours}} more for checklist, tests, variant and second review, about {{pilot_hours_per}} expert hours per sample, {{pilot_hours_total}} in all.
data.more_title: How it targets each gap, and three uses (evaluate, train, guard)

A: the checklist lists every required level, measure and column; the deficient variant drops one
to deliver every required level, not only the totals
B: the checklist marks which labels the prompt fixes and which only the rubric names, scored separately
to keep a label exact where the prompt fixes it
C: the checklist maps each required control or test condition to where it must appear; a judge check, validated on the complete / deficient pairs, tests it
to cover every specified case and control
D: accounting rules, such as no unsupported adjustments, are checklist entries with tests
to respect accounting rules the task implies (low priority: {{d_tasks_word}} occurrence)

uses: Score completeness against the checklist separately from numerical accuracy, and items in the prompt separately from rubric-only ones.
Expert deliverables as demonstrations; complete versus deficient pairs for preference training; the automated tests as rewards for reinforcement learning.
Rerun as a regression suite on each new model version.

pilot_plan._about: Parameters of the proposed pilot (proposal, not measured). The expert time per task is GDPval's reported average; the extra hours per sample are this proposal's estimate.
pilot_plan.gdpval_source: GDPval paper (arXiv:2510.04374v1), section 1: "Tasks require an average of 7 hours of work for an expert professional to complete."

items: Observed failure

GPT-6.1-sol, weekly sales analysis, rubric items {{card_a_items}}: 'Sales by Store' holds every store-brand row and a grand total that reconciles to the source, but no store subtotal rows, although the prompt asks the tab to "total the sales by store"; the store-level view cannot be read without re-aggregating. Claude Opus 5.5's workbook carries a labelled total for each of the {{stores}} stores.
Task input

a weekly sales export ({{source_rows}} rows: store, brand, WTD / MTD / YTD sales quantity, sales dollars and stock on hand) and the instruction to build brand and store summaries with sell-through as pivot tables.
Business rule
a store-level view carries one labelled subtotal per store equal to the sum of its brand rows, and a grand total equal to the sum of the subtotals; sell-through is the ratio of sums at each level.
Checklist (excerpt)

Sales by Store is a pivot table built from the Data tab (in the prompt); a labelled total for each store and a grand total equal to their sum (in the prompt: "total the sales by store", "include grand totals"; rubric items {{card_a_items}}); ST% = sales ÷ stock on hand at every level (in the prompt), computed from the totals, not averaged over rows (an evaluator's rule).
Target deliverable
on the Sales by Store tab, a pivot table built from the Data tab with Store and Brand as row fields, a labelled total under each store block and a grand total, each reconciling to the export.
Automated test

Sales by Store holds a pivot table whose source is the Data tab; for each of the {{stores}} stores a labelled total equal to the independent recomputation from the export; the grand total equal to the sum of the store totals; ST% within 0.0005 of the ratio of sums; expected values computed from the source, not read from the deliverable.
Why verified

GDPval's own expert file for this task fails two of these tests: its ST% averages row ratios (Clinique WTD {{gold_st_expert}} against {{gold_st_sums}} from the totals), and its Data tab differs from the source export in {{gold_cells}} cells, a difference the audit could not explain (an expert edit or another input version).
Targeted failure type
dropping a requested aggregation level during presentation while the top-level totals stay correct.
Composition

the evaluation’s {{tasks}} tasks and {{occupations_word}} occupations (Order Clerks; Accountants and Auditors; Computer and Information Systems Managers) as the seed, extended with tasks of the same families built from real source data, each with an expert deliverable and its checklist.
Training use
complete / deficient pairs, the same task with and without the required level (the expert deliverable against a version that drops the level), labelled by the checklist.
Train / evaluation separation

within each family, training and held-out tasks use different source materials (no shared sales export, store list or rubric text); held-out tasks use the same frozen tests. A separate leave-one-family-out run measures transfer to a new family.
Hypothesis
Expert deliverables carrying every requested level, with the task’s checklist, raise level-presence pass rates on unseen same-family tasks without lowering top-line accuracy; untested.

method.heading: Method and limits
method.sub: A rubric-based diagnostic, not GDPval's expert-preference metric.
strip: {{tasks}} tasks, {{rubric_items}} rubric items, {{crit_total}} critical requirements, frozen before the runs
Graders never guess; author review only where it can change a verdict
Graders agree with the author on {{ag_det_n}} of {{ag_det_d}} (code grader) and {{ag_judge_n}} of {{ag_judge_d}} (LLM judge) audited rubric items
Descriptive only; one author; failure sources tagged after the runs; the additions rule decides {{rule_task_fail_per_model}} failed {{rule_task_word}} per model
tasks_line: All {{oc_tasks}} GDPval Order Clerks tasks plus {{other_tasks}} from accounting and IT, each adding a different deliverable (prepaid schedule, tour P&L, slide deck, UAT plan, cloud design) under the same two demands: rules traceable to the inputs, and detail, summary and narrative that agree. Candidates were excluded only for missing or contradictory materials.
tooling: Built with coding agents: Claude Code wrote the harness, graders, analysis and this page; OpenAI Codex reviewed the code independently (read-only) and drafted the failure triage.
method.steps_title: How it was measured, step by step
steps: **Rubric.** Each GDPval task comes with an expert rubric: a list of **rubric items**, each worth points, such as one requiring a subtotal row for each store. Each model faces {{rubric_items}} rubric items across the {{tasks}} tasks. Before any model ran, the author grouped the rubric items each task can't do without into **critical requirements**: {{crit_total}} in all, {{crit_min}} to {{crit_max}} per task, covering {{crit_items}} rubric items.

**Run.** Each model did each task once, with the same prompt, tools and offline sandbox, at high reasoning effort (the same label doesn't mean the same compute), up to {{max_tokens}} output tokens per request and a {{time_limit_words}} limit.

**Grade.** Each rubric item went to one **grader**: a code grader, an LLM judge or human visual review. Graders never guess: if one couldn't read the part of the file it needed, the verdict is **cannot assess**, not a fail (e.g. content inside a chart, or two columns that both look like the vendor).

**Review.** An AI draft (OpenAI Codex) first sorted the {{reviewed}} rubric items graded fail or cannot assess by likely cause. In **author review**, the author then reviewed {{ws_rows}} rubric items by hand: every failed or cannot-assess rubric item that could change a critical requirement's verdict, every likely model failure, and the one graded pass the blind audit found failing.
method.example: {{ex_crit_count}} critical requirements, with their rubric items paraphrased: **the right sheets** (such as a sheet named Sales by Store); **correct brand totals** (one row per brand; each value equals the sum of the source rows); **a store view with a subtotal per store** (a subtotal row for each store; the grand total equals the sum of the subtotals); and **correct sell-through** (WTD ST% = WTD sales quantity ÷ WTD stock on hand).
config: **Prepare.** Selected the {{tasks}} tasks, checked their source files, rubrics and expert references, and fixed the {{crit_total}} critical requirements in a preregistration.
**Calibrate.** Tuned the code graders on development runs, then tested them on held-out runs before freezing.
**Freeze.** Fixed the prompt, graders and configuration (tags freeze-v1-generation and freeze-v1-grading).

**Run.** `{{opus_id}}` (adaptive thinking, effort {{effort}}) and `{{gpt_id}}` (reasoning effort {{effort}}), {{attempts_word}} attempt per task, {{max_tokens}} output tokens per request, {{time_limit_words}} limit, up to {{max_retries}} retries on transport errors only; {{gen_date_long}}, {{gen_start}}–{{gen_end}} UTC.

**Grade.** Code graders recompute expected values from the source files; the LLM judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro) grades the rest from the relevant cells, pages and source values; human visual review covers charts and layout. Judging ran {{judge_start}}–{{judge_end}} UTC.

**Audit.** The author labelled {{sample_n}} rubric items blind (saved {{labels_saved}} UTC, before seeing results). The LLM judge's held-out validation ({{jv_agree}}) ran at the same time as the main judging.
**Review.** AI draft (OpenAI Codex, read-only) over the {{reviewed}} rubric items graded fail or cannot assess; author review of {{ws_rows}}, {{review_time}}, with cells and pages located by Claude.
method.design_title: Design choices (graders never guess, the expert reference as evidence, frozen verdicts, task pass as the headline)
design: "Cannot assess" instead of an inferred pass, so no hidden passes.
The expert reference is evidence too.
Expected values come from the source files, which exposed a rubric stricter than its reference (tour task).
Frozen verdicts, author decisions on top.
Every correction stays traceable, and review time goes only where it can change a verdict.
A deliverable counts only if every must-have holds; severity shows how bad each failure is. Trade-off: one exact-label miss fails a whole task.
method.review_title: Author review of {{ws_rows}} rubric items: {{seg0}} confirmed failures, {{seg1}} grader false fails, {{seg2}} cannot assess → pass, and {{seg3}} cannot assess → left (their critical requirement already fails on another rubric item).
method.review_scope_title: How the {{ws_rows}} were chosen, and what was not reviewed
review_scope: Of the {{reviewed}} rubric items graded fail or cannot assess, the {{rv_crit}} inside critical requirements and the {{rv_draft}} the AI draft suspected were model failures; plus {{rv_fp}} graded pass that the blind audit found failing. By graded verdict: {{rv_fail}} fail ({{seg1}} grader false fails, {{rv_conf_fail}} confirmed), {{rv_ca}} cannot assess ({{seg2}} pass, {{rv_vfail}} fail, {{seg3}} left) and the {{rv_fp}} pass.

{{nr_fail}} graded fail outside critical requirements (the AI draft: {{nr_fail_ffail}} grader false fails, {{nr_fail_amb}} ambiguous rubric items), {{nr_ca}} cannot assess outside critical requirements, and {{nr_visual}} visual items without a verdict plus {{nr_invalid}} invalid judge outputs.

OpenAI Codex (read-only) sorted the {{reviewed}} rubric items graded fail or cannot assess by likely cause. The author decided each of the {{ws_rows}} from the deliverable itself, or from cells and pages located by Claude, with the AI draft only as a second opinion.
The code grader looked for "on hand" and missed "On-Hand", so {{d08_items_word}} correct inventory totals were judged missing.
method.reliability_sub: Blind audit: the author labelled {{sample_n}} rubric items without seeing the verdicts, {{ag_det_d}} graded by the code grader and {{ag_judge_d}} by the LLM judge.
reliability_tiles: rubric items where the code grader agrees with the author
rubric items where the LLM judge agrees with the author
method.selection_note: The blind audit samples all rubric items, most of which pass. The {{rv_fail}} reviewed fails were chosen where a verdict could change ({{rv_fail_crit}}) or a model failure was suspected ({{rv_fail_draft}}), and grader errors turned out to cluster there (one missed "On-Hand" label alone made ten false fails), so {{gff_pct}}% describes those fails, not an overall grader error rate.
method.judge_note: The LLM judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro) was also validated on {{jv_d}} held-out test cases, all passing, so its ability to catch failures is untested.
limits: {{tasks}} tasks, {{runs_each_word}} run each: all {{oc_tasks}} GDPval Order Clerks tasks plus {{other_tasks}} selected accounting and IT tasks. Counts are descriptive, not a model ranking.
Grader false passes were checked only in the {{sample_n}}-item blind audit ({{fp_all_n}} in {{fp_all_d}} audited passes).
The author chose the {{crit_total}} critical requirements (fixed before the runs) and rated severity (after review).
